concepts.title: Meaning and Features of Controlling
concepts.definition: The managerial function of seeing that work actually follows the plans laid down, so that the organisation's resources are put to effective and efficient use in reaching its set goals.
concepts.key_idea: It is goal-oriented, pervasive across all levels and all kinds of organisations, and never merely the closing act -- by exposing deviations and their causes it feeds the next round of planning and thus completes one management cycle only to restart it.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 54-105 (Meaning of Controlling; pervasive and primary; not the last function)
question_patterns: state the meaning of controlling
why is controlling called a goal oriented function
is controlling the last function of management give reasons
controlling is a pervasive function justify
how does controlling complete one cycle of the management process
which function ensures that activities conform to the plans

solution_steps.explain: Controlling means ensuring that activities are performed as per the plans and that resources serve the predetermined goals.
It reaches every level of every organisation -- school, hospital, army or business -- and is a primary duty of each manager.
It is not the final function: the deviations it uncovers improve future plans, closing one cycle and opening the next.

concepts.title: Importance of Controlling
concepts.definition: The payoffs of a sound control system: it steers the organisation toward its goals by exposing deviations, tests whether the standards themselves are accurate, cuts wastage of resources, motivates employees who know how they will be judged, curbs dishonesty through close checking, and aligns every department behind one direction.
concepts.key_idea: Six benefits -- goal accomplishment, judging standards, efficient resource use, motivation, order and discipline, coordination in action.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 106-180 (Importance i-vi; computer monitoring case)
question_patterns: explain the importance of controlling in an organisation
how does controlling help in accomplishing organisational goals
which benefit of controlling lets managers revise their standards
how does a control system improve employee motivation
controlling ensures order and discipline discuss
how does controlling facilitate coordination in action

solution_steps.explain: Goal accomplishment, accuracy of standards, efficient use of resources, motivation, order and discipline, coordination.
For motivation: employees told in advance the standards they will be appraised on work with greater purpose.
Without control even the best plans drift; control keeps the organisation on its plotted course.

concepts.title: Limitations of Controlling
concepts.definition: The boundaries of the function: some standards such as morale or satisfaction resist measurement in numbers, external forces like government policy and technology stay beyond its reach, employees often resent being watched, and running a control system costs money, time and effort that a small firm may not justify.
concepts.key_idea: Four limitations -- hard-to-quantify standards, external factors, employee resistance, and cost; the rule is that control costs must never outstrip control benefits.
question_patterns: state the limitations of controlling
why does a control system lose effectiveness without quantitative standards
can an organisation control its external factors explain
why do employees resist control systems like cctv monitoring
is controlling a costly affair comment

solution_steps.explain: Difficulty in quantitative standards, little control over external factors, resistance from employees, costly affair.
Morale, satisfaction and behaviour cannot be expressed in numbers, so measuring and comparing them is hard.
The expense of installing and operating the system should stay below the benefits it brings.

concepts.title: Relationship between Planning and Controlling
concepts.definition: Two inseparable twins: planning supplies the standards that controlling measures performance against, and controlling feeds back what actually happened so that future plans improve -- each is meaningless without the other.
concepts.key_idea: Planning prescribes while controlling evaluates; planning looks ahead and controlling looks back, yet both face both ways -- plans draw on past experience and corrective action targets future performance.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 251-322 (Relationship between Planning and Controlling)
question_patterns: discuss the relationship between planning and controlling
planning is looking ahead and controlling is looking back comment
why is controlling blind without planning
planning is prescriptive while controlling is evaluative explain
how does controlling improve future planning
are planning and controlling inseparable twins justify

solution_steps.action: State the dependence of control on plans
solution_steps.explain: Standards set by planning are the benchmarks; with no plan there is nothing to control.
Deviations found by controlling become information that sharpens the next plan.

solution_steps.action: Handle the looking ahead or back line
solution_steps.explain: The saying is only partly right: each function is both backward-looking and forward-looking.

concepts.title: Steps in the Controlling Process
concepts.definition: Five ordered steps: set the performance standards in precise, preferably quantitative terms, measure the actual performance objectively through observation, sample checking or reports, compare it with the standards, analyse the deviations that cross the acceptable range and find their causes, and finally take corrective action or revise the standards.
concepts.key_idea: Standards may be quantitative like cost, units and time, or qualitative like goodwill; measurement works best in the same units as the standard, and comparison exposes the deviation.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 323-618 (Controlling Process steps 1-5, standards table, sample checking)
question_patterns: explain the various steps involved in the process of control
which standards can a firm set for its finance department

what is sample checking and where is it used
when is corrective action taken in the control process
what should a manager do when deviations cannot be corrected

solution_steps.action: List the five steps in order
solution_steps.explain: Setting standards, measuring actual performance, comparing with standards, analysing deviations, taking corrective action.
Personal observation, sample checking and performance reports give objective readings; small firms check every piece, large firms sample.

solution_steps.action: Describe the analysis and the response
solution_steps.explain: Deviations beyond the acceptable range are traced to causes -- defective process, inadequate resources, unrealistic standards -- then corrected by training, extra resources, or revision of the standard itself.

concepts.title: Measuring Deviation from Standards
concepts.definition: The arithmetic heart of step three and four: the gap between what was actually achieved and what the standard demanded shows the deviation, and expressing it as a percentage of the standard tells the manager how serious it is relative to the acceptable range.
concepts.key_idea: A positive figure means performance ran above standard, a negative one below; only deviations beyond the permissible limit, such as labour cost rising past the allowed 2 per cent, reach the manager.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 364-391 and 464-543 (setting precise standards, acceptable range of deviation, critical limits)
question_patterns: calculate the percentage deviation when actual performance is {actual_performance} against a standard of {standard_performance}
a firm's labour cost rose from a standard of {standard_performance} to {actual_performance} find the deviation percentage
actual output was {actual_performance} units against a standard of {standard_performance} units compute the deviation as a percentage
how far did performance deviate from the standard in percentage terms
is the deviation within the acceptable range of 2 per cent compute and decide

solution_steps.action: Take the gap between actual and standard
solution_steps.explain: Subtract the standard from the actual figure to get the absolute deviation.

solution_steps.action: Express the gap as a percentage of the standard
solution_steps.explain: Dividing by the standard and multiplying by 100 makes deviations of any size comparable against the permissible limit.

worked_examples.question: Using Measuring Deviation from Standards, compute the result for actual_performance = 3, standard_performance = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between actual and standard: gap = actual_performance - standard_performance = 0.0 Step 2: Express the gap as a percentage of the standard: percentage_deviation = gap / standard_performance * 100 = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Take the gap between actual and standard: gap = actual_performance - standard_performance = 0.0 Step 2: Express the gap as a percentage of the standard: percentage_deviation = gap / standard_performance * 100 = 0.0 Final result: 0.0

concepts.title: Critical Point Control and Management by Exception
concepts.definition: Two companion principles for step four: critical point control concentrates attention on the key result areas whose failure would hurt the whole organisation, and management by exception escalates only the significant deviations that cross the permissible limit, leaving routine variance to subordinates.
concepts.key_idea: Controlling everything controls nothing; a 5 per cent labour-cost rise may matter more than a 15 per cent rise in postal charges -- the advantages are saved time, focus on vital areas, easier delegation and timely action on critical problems.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 464-568 (critical point control, management by exception, advantages box)
question_patterns: an effort to control everything may end up in controlling nothing explain
what is meant by critical point control
which principle should a manager apply while dealing with deviations
a worker falls short of target by ten units should the ceo intervene explain with the relevant principle
state the advantages of management by exception
what are key result areas in controlling

solution_steps.explain: The case of a minor shortfall escalated to the top calls for management by exception.
Only deviations beyond the permissible limit in key result areas reach higher management; the rest stay with subordinates.
Managers save time, focus on vital matters, delegate routine checks and act on critical problems in time -- so the CEO need not act on a ten-unit shortfall.

concepts.title: Techniques of Managerial Control
concepts.definition: The manager's toolkit falls in two shelves: traditional techniques -- breakeven analysis, personal observation, statistical reports and budgetary control -- and modern techniques -- ratio analysis, return on investment, management audit, PERT and CPM, responsibility accounting, and the management information system.
concepts.key_idea: Breakeven analysis finds the no-profit-no-loss point, budgetary control runs the firm against quantified plans, PERT and CPM schedule networked projects, and a management audit reviews the whole managerial apparatus rather than one post.
concepts.textbook_ref: lebs108.txt lines 624-658 (Key terms and summary lists of traditional and modern techniques)
question_patterns: name the traditional and modern techniques of managerial control
how does management audit serve as an effective technique of controlling
what does breakeven analysis show a manager

how does budgetary control work as a technique
what is the role of a management information system in controlling

solution_steps.action: Sort the technique into its shelf
solution_steps.explain: Observation, statistical reports, breakeven analysis and budgetary control are traditional; ROI, ratio analysis, responsibility accounting, management audit, PERT, CPM and MIS are modern.
For instance, a management audit evaluates the total performance of the management process itself, not just one function.
Each technique watches a different variable -- costs, schedules, returns or managerial quality.

worked_examples.source_ref: lebs108.txt lines 516-528 (2 per cent acceptable range for labour cost)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A plant budgeted labour cost of {standard_performance} thousand rupees but actually spent {actual_performance} thousand. Compute the percentage deviation and say whether it crosses a 2 per cent acceptable range.

solution_template.action: Take the gap between actual and standard
solution_template.explain: 515 minus 500 gives a rise of 15 thousand rupees.

solution_template.action: Express the gap as a percentage of the standard
solution_template.explain: 15 divided by 500, times 100, gives 3 per cent -- beyond the 2 per cent limit, so it goes to management.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A worker misses his daily production target by 10 units on two consecutive days and the production head asks the CEO to terminate him. Which principle of control should the CEO apply while deciding?

solution_template.explain: Management by exception -- only significant deviations beyond the permissible limit deserve top-level action.
A ten-unit daily shortfall is a small, routine deviation for the worker's own supervisor to handle.
The CEO should decline termination and let the deviation be examined at the appropriate lower level.

worked_examples.question_pattern: A chief manager instructs the production head to keep a constant check that everything goes per plan and to track every employee's performance so targets are met. Which features of controlling does this highlight?

solution_template.explain: Checking that work follows the set plan shows controlling is goal-oriented; the demand for constant and continuous check shows it is a continuous process.
Goal-oriented function and continuous (also pervasive, since every employee falls under the check).
Tracking performance against targets ties the function directly to goal attainment, and its reach across all staff shows pervasiveness.
